did_you_know.text: In the ancient world, some people showed mourning by cutting their skin or shaving part of their heads. The Torah forbids these mourning customs.
The phrase “a treasured people” describes a people with a special status and responsibility, not a claim that it is better than all other nations. The choice is connected with Israel’s role.
The modern identification of several animals named in this verse is uncertain. That is why different translations sometimes give different animal names.
According to the verse, a permitted land animal has two signs: split hooves and chewing the cud. Together, these signs distinguish it from other animals.
The Torah gives fins and scales as signs of fish that may be eaten. Fins help a fish move, while scales protect its body.
The identification of some birds in this chapter, such as the peres and the ozniah, is uncertain. This is one reason translations and modern bird lists sometimes differ.
The Hebrew name for the stork, chasidah, is related to the word chesed, meaning kindness. Jewish tradition has offered different explanations for this name.
The prohibition against cooking a young goat in its mother’s milk appears three times in the Torah. The Sages developed from it the broader laws separating meat and dairy.
The tithe brought to Jerusalem is called ma’aser sheni, or “second tithe,” in rabbinic literature. It was not simply a tax; it was eaten in holiness at the Temple site.
When the journey to Jerusalem was too long to carry the produce, the Torah allowed it to be exchanged for money. The money could then be spent in Jerusalem on food and drink.
